extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers (readers of Montaigne, interested in philosophy, medicine, and moral reflection)
extracted.subtask_description: Personal/reflective essay exploring skepticism toward professions (especially medicine), practical wisdom, and the relation of action to reputation; mixes anecdote, aphorism, and philosophical argument. Useful as a model for first‑person moral or philosophical essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of medical certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: 'for it is almost impossible but he must often fall into those mistakes' — physicians must account for many variables (complexion, temperament, humours, external circumstances, planets, causes, prognostics, drugs' provenance and composition), making error almost inevitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why medicine is uncertain: multitude of interacting factors; examples of diagnostic disagreement ('I never found three of one opinion'); anecdotal surgical errors. Anti‑pattern: claiming certainty where complexity exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for observable, tactile methods (surgery over conjectural medicine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Surgery is 'much more certain, by reason that it sees and feels what it does,' whereas physicians lack a 'speculum' to inspect internal organs and must rely on conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses concrete examples (cases of mistaken diagnosis revealed on autopsy) to argue that methods which rely on direct observation are more reliable than those built on inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about compound remedies' selective actions
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Of all this bundle of things having mixed up a potion, is it not a kind of madness to imagine or to hope that these differing virtues should separate themselves from one another in this mixture and confusion...' — compound medicines cannot be relied on to send different 'virtues' to different organs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy of tickets and messengers: mixing ingredients likely causes interaction, corruption, or loss of intended effects. Anti‑pattern: asserting precise organ‑targeting effects of complex mixtures without mechanism or evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization over general practice
rubrics_metrics.description: 'he who provides for all, provides for nothing' — professions (including medicine) perform better when divided, with specific practitioners for particular diseases or body parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to tailors and cooks; historical reference to Egyptian practice. Implication for practice: favor focused expertise rather than a one‑size‑all practitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of inconsistency and paradox in medical counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical advice often offers contradictory recommendations (e.g., bathing often vs not, frequent sex both good and bad, drinking and not drinking at specific times), revealing lack of coherent rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses multiple paired contradictions to show unreliability; suggests caution when following prescriptive regimens that contradict themselves depending on minor contextual shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for simple, natural remedies and modest claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Baths and other simple, natural practices 'carry no danger with them, though they may do us no good' — prefer remedies with low risk and modest, honest claims rather than miraculous promises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounded in Montaigne's personal experience with baths; warns against extravagant miracle stories and the gullibility that accepts them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about anecdotal or chance‑driven experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Most claimed cures derived from chance or single observations are unreliable: 'how many times was it repeated... and when the rule is concluded, by whom?' — experience requires systematic, repeated observation and transparent recordation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that one or few experiments, especially without controls or repetition, cannot establish reliable medical rules; calls out reliance on 'fortune' or isolated witnesses as insufficient evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand transparency and broader evidence before trusting authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unreasonable that 'three doctors' should dictate to all mankind; medical claims should be supported by wider testimony and open records of judgments and experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for disclosure of all judgments and arguments rather than deference to a small authoritative clique; anti‑pattern: accepting expert claims without accessible evidence or provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware practitioners who do not practice what they preach
rubrics_metrics.description: Physicians often prescribe diets and regimens that they themselves do not follow, which undermines the credibility of their prescriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use practitioners' personal conduct as a heuristic for trustworthiness; anti‑pattern: admiring or following advice from those who clearly flout their own rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid impatience and the appetite for immediate cures
rubrics_metrics.description: '‘Tis pure cowardice that makes our belief so pliable and easy to be imposed upon' — fear of death and impatience lead patients to accept doubtful cures; patience is often the better course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages restraint and skepticism in seeking quick fixes; example of mass gullibility and the social pressure to accept remedies. Anti‑pattern: trading prudence for rash acceptance of any promised remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overvalue posthumous reputation; value practical usefulness in life
rubrics_metrics.description: 'I am not at all ambitious that any one should love and esteem me more dead than living' — prefer to be useful through conduct and action rather than to seek fame after death through writings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advises authors/thinkers to prioritize real‑world usefulness and present conduct over literary legacy; 'studies to teach me to do, and not to write.' Anti‑pattern: sacrificing practical competence for the sake of producing reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of study: practical application over literary display
rubrics_metrics.description: 'My studies, to teach me to do, and not to write' — education and study should prepare one to act, not merely to produce texts for posterity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages evaluating scholarship and learning by its capacity to enable action and conduct; anti‑pattern: valuing rhetorical skill or posthumous glory above actual competence and virtue.
